title: Four Classical Losses in Eight Rounds. Magnus Carlsen Is Second-to-Last at Norway Chess. Praggnanandhaa Has Beaten Him Twice.
excerpt: The five-time world champion has nine points with two rounds left. Wesley So leads with fourteen. Carlsen's worst classical run in years has turned Oslo into someone else's tournament.
body:
There is a word for what is happening to Magnus Carlsen in Oslo, and the commentators at Norway Chess have started using it carefully: cliche. Not the word itself, but the feeling around his defeats. By the time Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu beat him for the second time in Round 8, it no longer produced the shock that a Carlsen loss once carried.

Four classical losses in eight rounds. The five-time World Champion — still the World No. 1 by rating — sits on nine points, second-to-last in a six-player field, ahead of only World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju. With two rounds remaining, he is mathematically alive but practically finished in the title race.

## How It Unravelled

Carlsen's tournament started with a loss to Alireza Firouzja in Round 1 and never stabilised. He bounced back with a win over Firouzja in Round 3 and beat him again in Round 6, but those victories were sandwiched between classical defeats that kept pulling him backward.

In Round 4, Praggnanandhaa beat him with the white pieces in a complex middlegame. In Round 5, Wesley So dismantled him. In Round 8, Praggnanandhaa did it again — this time with black, in a French Defence where Carlsen had white and was ostensibly trying to avenge the earlier defeat.

The game lasted 50 moves. Carlsen chose an aggressive setup but burned time in the opening phase. By move 14, he had moved his king to f1 — an unusual commitment that left his kingside vulnerable. Praggnanandhaa accepted structural damage early but gained active piece play and central control. Black's rooks, bishops, and queen coordinated relentlessly, and Carlsen's position eroded under time pressure.

The decisive error came on move 48. Carlsen played Kf4, walking into a forced mating pattern. Ke2 would have held. The audience in Oslo fell silent. Praggnanandhaa did not celebrate.

"It's more important for the tournament that I get this win than thinking that it's Magnus," the 20-year-old said afterward. "Of course, it's great to do it against Magnus, but I think winning any game at this stage of the tournament is good."

ChessBase India noted that this was the third time Praggnanandhaa had beaten Carlsen at Norway Chess, and the second time this year.

## The Standings After Round 8

Wesley So leads with 14 points. Alireza Firouzja is second with 13. Praggnanandhaa sits third with 12. Vincent Keymer has 10. Carlsen has 9. Gukesh, the reigning World Champion, trails with 8.

So, the Filipino-American grandmaster, has led since Round 6 and extended his advantage with a Round 8 armageddon win over Keymer. He has not lost a classical game in the tournament. His strategy has been to draw in classical and win in armageddon — not the most glamorous approach, but devastatingly effective under Norway Chess's scoring system.

He acknowledged as much. "I'd like to apologize," he told the crowd before Round 8. "Of course, I'd like to fight in the classical games, but it's not so easy to get an opening advantage." His lead, built on consistency rather than brilliance, has held because no one else has been consistent enough to challenge him.

## Firouzja's Resilience

Firouzja occupies second place with 13 points, just one behind So, after beating World Champion Gukesh in a rook endgame in Round 8. The French grandmaster has had a volatile tournament — he lost two consecutive classical games in Rounds 6-7 to Carlsen and Praggnanandhaa respectively — but responded with a classical win over Gukesh that keeps his title hopes alive heading into the final two rounds.

If So draws both remaining classical games and loses both armageddons, Firouzja could overtake him with two classical wins. It is unlikely but not impossible. The margin is thin enough to sustain interest.

## Praggnanandhaa's Rise

The 20-year-old from Chennai is the story of the tournament's second half. After losing to both So and Gukesh in the early rounds, he has won three of his last four classical games — beating Carlsen, Firouzja, and Carlsen again. His Round 7 demolition of Firouzja was a 3-0 sweep: classical win followed by an armageddon that never happened because Firouzja had already lost the full three points.

With 12 points, Praggnanandhaa sits two behind So. He cannot win the tournament outright without So faltering, but a strong finish would cement his status as the most dangerous classical player of the younger generation. His form here is arguably more impressive than Gukesh's, given that the World Champion has struggled with four losses and sits last.

## What It Means for Indian Chess

Norway Chess 2026 features three players of Indian origin in its six-player field — Gukesh, Praggnanandhaa, and Wesley So, who was born in the Philippines and represents the United States. For Indian chess fans watching from the diaspora, the tournament tells two stories: Praggnanandhaa's emergence as a genuine elite-level classical threat, and Gukesh's uncharacteristic struggle in his first major event as World Champion.

The tournament runs through June 5 in Oslo. Rounds 9 and 10 will determine whether So can secure his first major classical tournament victory, whether Firouzja can mount a last-day charge, and whether Praggnanandhaa can overtake Firouzja for second.

For Carlsen, the remaining question is simpler: can he avoid finishing last? It would be the worst result in his professional career at a round-robin super-tournament. The man who dominated chess for over a decade is now fighting to avoid a humiliation he once would have considered unthinkable.

Norway Chess uses a unique format where drawn classical games are followed by an armageddon tiebreak. A classical win earns 3 points. An armageddon win earns 1.5 points. An armageddon loss earns 1 point. A classical loss earns 0. The format rewards fighting chess — which makes Carlsen's repeated classical losses all the more damaging.
